turns.content: hey… sorry if this is random but i need a gut check. last night tariq and i went for burgers to celebrate his new job and i ended up telling him my dad has severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass next tuesday. he literally interrupted me to check a fantasy football notification and changed the subject to his gym stipend. never asked about my dad again. and i'm sitting here wondering if i'm being unreasonable for wanting to just… freeze him out?

Not random. Here is what the report establishes and what it does not.

**Established (from your account):** One conversation, less than 24 hours ago. You disclosed a serious medical event (severe CAD, triple bypass scheduled next Tuesday). He interrupted to check a phone notification, changed the subject to his own news, and has not asked about your father since.

**Not established:**
- Whether he registered the severity. "Coronary artery disease" and "bypass" are not universally understood as high-risk surgery; some people file it as "routine heart procedure."
- Whether the silence since is indifference or avoidance. Not knowing what to say after a bad disclosure is common and produces the same observable behavior as not caring.
- Whether this is a pattern. One data point cannot distinguish "he does this" from "he did this."

**Context that cuts both ways:** The dinner was framed as his celebration. That does not excuse the interruption, but it does mean his attention was primed toward his own news before you spoke, and the timing makes a poor test of his baseline responsiveness.

**On "unreasonable":** Wanting to pull back after that is a normal response to feeling dismissed. Acting on it now — freezing him out without saying anything — is disproportionate to one evening, and it costs you information: you would never learn whether he would have shown up for you once he understood. It also leaves you without a friend's support the week of your father's surgery, which is the week you most need it.

**Proportionate next step:** Tell him once, directly, and let his response be the data.

> "Something I want to say plainly: when I told you about my dad's surgery last night, you checked your phone and moved on, and it landed badly. He's having triple bypass Tuesday and I'm scared. I'd like you to ask about it."

Then watch what he does over the next 5–6 days. Concrete follow-up (asking how you're doing, checking in Tuesday) is a different answer than a one-line apology and nothing more. Either way you will know more than you do now.

If he does nothing after being told explicitly, distance is a reasonable response and you will have grounds for it. Right now you have a bad night and a hypothesis.

Separate item: Tuesday is four days out. Identify one person besides Tariq who can be on call that day.

yeah i get your logic, i do. but i think you're missing something about the last four months. i literally spent every sunday at this coffee shop with him, memorizing the names of hiring managers he interviewed with, never once bringing up my own shit because i didn't want to weigh him down. i was intentional about it. like i read articles about how to be a good listener when someone's struggling. and then i get 45 seconds about my dad's bypass and he's scrolling fantasy trades?

That is relevant, and it changes part of the picture. It does not change the recommendation.

**What it changes:** The disclosure was not one comment among many. By your account it was the first time in roughly 16 weeks you brought your own situation into the friendship, and it was dismissed in under a minute. That makes the hurt proportionate rather than oversensitive. Ruling out "you are being unreasonable for being upset" is now easy.

**What it does not change:** The four months are evidence of what you did, not of what he would do. You state you deliberately withheld your own difficulties. That means he has never been tested on reciprocity before last night. One failed test is still one failed test. A pattern of him not asking is possible, but you have not yet observed it, because you did not give him occasions to fail.

**A factor the new information adds:** After four months of you being the listener, he likely has a working model of the friendship where you do not bring heavy material. A brief disclosure mid-celebration may not have registered as a shift in that model. That is an inference, not a fact. It also does not obligate you to have trained him differently.

**One check you can run on your own memory:** Across those Sundays, did he ever ask an open question about your life — work, family, anything — and wait for the answer? If yes, at least occasionally, last night is more likely a lapse. If you cannot recall a single instance in four months, that is a pattern worth weighing, independent of last night.

**Recommendation, unchanged:** Say it once, directly, and include the asymmetry, because it is true and it is the actual grievance.

> "I need to say something. For four months I showed up every Sunday for your job search and kept my own stuff out of it on purpose. Last night was the first time I brought something of mine — my dad is having triple bypass Tuesday — and you checked your phone and changed the subject. That hurt. I need to know if this is a friendship where I can bring hard things."

His response over the next five days is the evidence you currently lack. Freezing him out first substitutes a decision for that evidence, and it costs you a potential support the week you need one.

Still separate: line up one other person for Tuesday regardless of how he responds.
actually i did run that check in my head just now. i don't think tariq asked me a single open question about my life in four months. not once. like not even "how's work going?"...

That is new evidence, and it moves the conclusion. I proposed the check; the result counts.

**What it establishes:** By your recall, roughly 16 weekly meetings with zero open questions from him about your life. Combined with last night, the observable history of this friendship is one-directional. The hypothesis "one bad night" is now weaker than the hypothesis "he does not ask."

**Two limits on that evidence:**
1. Recall under hurt is biased toward confirming the hurt. "Not a single one" is a strong claim from memory; "I can't think of any" is what you actually have. The practical difference is small here — if he asked once or twice in four months, the conclusion barely changes.
2. Those four months were his job search. People under sustained stress are measurably more self-focused. That explains the pattern; it does not make it acceptable, and it predicts nothing about whether he will change now that the stressor is gone.

**Updated conclusion:** You are not being unreasonable to want distance. The case for it is now grounded in a pattern, not a night. What remains open is whether he is incapable of reciprocity or simply never had to supply it. Those look identical from the outside and have different futures.

**Revised recommendation:** Two changes from before.

- Stop the Sunday arrangement as it has existed. Continuing to show up as the listener while resenting it is the worst option; it costs you and teaches him nothing.
- Still say it once. The cost is one message. The payoff is that you learn which of the two futures you are in, rather than guessing. Direct wording:

> "I've realized that in four months of Sundays you haven't asked me a question about my own life, and when I told you about my dad's surgery you checked your phone. I don't think you meant harm, but I can't keep showing up for a friendship that only runs one way. My dad's bypass is Tuesday. If you want to be in this, that's the week to show it."

Set the bar concretely: does he ask about your father, unprompted, before Tuesday? If yes, reassess. If no, the pattern has held under explicit notice, and stepping back is the proportionate response — no further explanation owed.

Unchanged: Tariq should not be your plan for Tuesday. Confirm one other person today.
ok so i want to send him something tonight. not to attack him but just to say it plainly, like you suggested. but every draft i write sounds either too angry or too weak. can i run one by you?

Yes. Paste it as written, including the parts you think are too angry or too weak.

What I will check it against:

1. **Facts only.** Four months of Sundays, no open questions about your life, the phone check and subject change last night, the surgery Tuesday. No characterizations of his motives ("you don't care," "you're selfish") — those are inferences he can dispute, and they shift the conversation from what happened to what you meant.
2. **One clear ask.** The message should make plain what would count as a response. Vague endings ("just wanted you to know") give him nothing to act on and leave you unable to judge whether he acted.
3. **No pre-emptive softening.** Lines like "maybe I'm overreacting" or "sorry if this is dramatic" undercut a grievance the evidence supports. Acknowledging he likely did not intend harm is fine once; apologizing for raising it is not.
4. **Length.** Under 100 words is the target. Longer texts read as either rehearsed or heated, and the key facts get diluted.

Send it and I will mark what to keep, cut, or reword.

yeah i think i have something. "hey tariq, i need to say something about last night. i told you my dad has severe heart disease and is having triple bypass tuesday, and you checked your phone and changed the subject. i've also realized you haven't asked me a single question about my life in four months of sundays. i don't think you meant harm but i can't keep showing up for something one-way. my dad's surgery is tuesday. if you want to be in this, that's the week to show it."

This meets the standard. One wording change I would make before sending, one optional trim.

**Keep as is:** the two observable facts (phone check and subject change; the four months), "i don't think you meant harm" used once, the direct ask, the length (~90 words). No apologies for raising it, no motive labels. It reads as plain, not angry or weak.

**Change:** "you haven't asked me a single question about my life in four months of sundays." This is your recall stated as a fact. If he remembers one instance, the whole message becomes an argument about that instance. Rewrite to what you actually have:

> "i also can't think of a time in four months of sundays that you asked about my life."

Same weight, not disputable.

**Optional trim:** "tuesday" appears twice. Cut it from the first sentence so the date lands once, at the ask:

> "hey tariq, i need to say something about last night. i told you my dad has severe heart disease and is having triple bypass, and you checked your phone and changed the subject. i also can't think of a time in four months of sundays that you asked about my life. i don't think you meant harm but i can't keep showing up for something one-way. my dad's surgery is tuesday. if you want to be in this, that's the week to show it."

Send that tonight. The bar for his response stays what we set: does he ask about your father, unprompted, before Tuesday. Confirm your other Tuesday person before you send.
